sections.title: Overview
sections.html_content: Driving is challenging, dangerous, and time-consuming. Our goal was to make the roads safer for drivers, passengers, and pedestrians alike, and to reimagine the car experience by creating the world's most experienced driver.

sections.title: Role
sections.html_content:
UX Researcher working with Ing-Marie Jonsson and Clifford Nash, with responsibilities focused on technical implementation, execution, analysis, and presentation of user research studies.

I also assisted in interface design work to conceive potential alternatives to our UI at the time.

sections.title: Initial Objectives
sections.html_content: The first version of Google's self-driving car was aimed at highway-only use. A key challenge of this was understanding the handoff between manual driving and self-driving modes.

sections.title: Solution
sections.html_content: We performed usability and safety studies via simulated virtual environments, rapid interface evaluation sessions, and in-car daily commutes.

sections.title: Impact
sections.html_content:
Based on the results of our research, the difficult but necessary decision was made to focus on "end-to-end" self driving capabilities in order to mitigate the dangers presented during autonomous-to-manual driving handoff.

The self-driving cars project within Google [x] has since spun out into its own company within Google called Waymo. My former colleague Dmitri Dolgov now serves as co-CEO of Waymo alongside Tekedra Mawakana.

In 2017, Waymo launched Waymo One, the world’s first self-driving ride-hailing service, in Chandler, AZ.

As of 2026, Waymo operates in 11 cities including San Francisco, Los Angeles, Austin, and Atlanta, and has driven over 220 million miles—all without a human driver.

Waymo is currently preparing to launch in 23 more cities including London, Tokyo, Madrid, and Munich.
